name: Judges

overview.author: Not stated. Jewish tradition credits Samuel. The repeated line “in those days there was no king in Israel” suggests it was written early in the monarchy.
overview.date: The events span roughly 1380–1050 BC, between Joshua’s death and the rise of Saul. It was likely written around 1000 BC.
overview.audience: Israel in the early monarchy, to show why the nation needed a righteous king and how dangerous it is to abandon God.
overview.setting: Canaan during roughly three centuries of tribal life, with no central government and constant threats from surrounding peoples.
overview.purpose: To show the destructive cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance, to display God’s patient mercy in raising up judges, and to expose the need for a faithful king.
overview.structure: An introduction showing incomplete conquest and the cycle (1:1–3:6), the stories of twelve judges (3:7–16:31), and two epilogues showing Israel’s moral collapse (17–21).

items.title: Failure to drive out the Canaanites

outline.title: Epilogue: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes

items.title: The Levite’s concubine and civil war

themes.title: The Cycle of Sin
themes.text: Israel sins, God allows oppression, Israel cries out, God raises a deliverer, and there is peace until they sin again (2:11–19).

themes.title: God’s Patient Mercy
themes.text: Again and again God hears His people’s cry and rescues them, even when their repentance is shallow.

themes.title: Flawed Deliverers
themes.text: God uses weak and flawed people like a left-handed man, a fearful farmer, an outcast, and a reckless strongman.

themes.title: The Spirit of the LORD
themes.text: The Spirit empowers judges for deliverance (3:10; 6:34; 14:6).

themes.title: Moral Relativism
themes.text: “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25) leads to idolatry, violence, and chaos.

themes.title: The Need for a King
themes.text: The book points to Israel’s need for a righteous king, ultimately Christ.

christInBook.text: Each judge is a partial, flawed savior who points to the perfect Deliverer.
Samson, a Nazirite from birth, begins to save Israel and wins his greatest victory in his death (compare Hebrews 2:14–15).
The cry for a king is answered in David and ultimately in Jesus, the righteous King (Isaiah 9:6–7).
Gideon’s altar “The LORD Is Peace” points to Christ, our peace (Ephesians 2:14).

crossReferences.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah in the hall of faith.
Paul summarizes the period of the judges.
Israel’s mingling with the nations and God’s compassion.

reflection: Where do you see the cycle of Judges (drifting, trouble, crying out, rescue) in your own life?
Gideon felt like the least in his family, yet God called him a mighty man of valor. How does God see you differently than you see yourself?
Samson’s strength was undone by compromise. What small compromises could grow into bigger falls for you?
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” Where are you following your own judgment rather than God’s word?
God used flawed people. How does that encourage you to serve despite your weaknesses?

chapterList.title: Incomplete Conquest
chapterList.summary: After Joshua’s death, Judah and Simeon have success, and Caleb’s family takes Hebron and Debir. But tribe after tribe fails to drive out the Canaanites, settling to live among them or put them to forced labor.
questions: What pattern do you notice as the chapter goes on?
Why was partial obedience so dangerous for Israel?
What areas of your life show “partial obedience”?

chapterList.title: Israel’s Unfaithfulness and the Cycle
chapterList.summary: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bochim for making covenants with the Canaanites. A new generation arises “who did not know the LORD.” The cycle is introduced: Israel serves the Baals, God gives them to enemies, then raises up judges to save them, but they keep turning away.
questions: How can a whole generation grow up not knowing the LORD (2:10)?
Describe the cycle in 2:11–19 in your own words.
Why does God continue to rescue such an unfaithful people?

chapterList.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
chapterList.summary: God leaves nations to test Israel. Othniel, empowered by the Spirit, delivers Israel from Mesopotamia. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, kills fat King Eglon of Moab with a hidden sword. Shamgar strikes down 600 Philistines with an oxgoad.
questions: Why did God leave nations in the land (3:1–4)?
How does God use Ehud’s left-handedness?
What unusual “tools” has God given you to use for Him?

chapterList.title: Deborah and Barak
chapterList.summary: Israel is oppressed by Jabin and his commander Sisera with 900 iron chariots. The prophetess Deborah, who judges Israel, summons Barak, who will only go if she goes. God routs Sisera, who flees and is killed by Jael with a tent peg.
questions: What do you notice about Deborah’s leadership?
Why did Barak lose the honor (4:9), and yet he is in Hebrews 11:32?
How does God use unexpected people to bring victory?

chapterList.title: The Song of Deborah
chapterList.summary: Deborah and Barak sing praise to God for the victory, celebrating the volunteers who offered themselves, criticizing tribes that stayed home, and blessing Jael. The stars and the river Kishon fought against Sisera.
questions: Why does the song praise the people who “offered themselves willingly” (5:2, 9)?
What does the criticism of Reuben, Dan, and Asher teach about staying uninvolved?
How does the song close (5:31)?

chapterList.title: Gideon Called
chapterList.summary: Midian oppresses Israel for seven years. The angel of the LORD finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress and calls him “mighty man of valor.” Gideon builds an altar named “The LORD Is Peace,” tears down his father’s Baal altar, and asks for signs with the fleece.
questions: Why do you think God called Gideon “mighty man of valor” while he was hiding?
Why was tearing down the family altar the first step?
What do you think of Gideon’s fleece test? How should we seek guidance?

chapterList.title: Gideon’s Three Hundred
chapterList.summary: God reduces Gideon’s army from 32,000 to 300 “lest Israel boast.” Gideon overhears a Midianite’s dream that confirms victory. With trumpets, jars, and torches, the 300 shout, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” and Midian flees in confusion.
questions: Why did God reduce Gideon’s army?
How does God strengthen Gideon’s faith through the overheard dream?
Where might God be “reducing” your resources so that His power is seen?

chapterList.title: Gideon Pursues Midian; the Ephod
chapterList.summary: Gideon calms the Ephraimites with a gentle answer, punishes Succoth and Penuel, and captures the Midianite kings. He refuses to be king, saying, “The LORD will rule over you,” but makes a golden ephod that becomes a snare to Israel.
questions: How does Gideon’s soft answer (8:1–3) defuse conflict?
Why did Gideon’s ephod become a snare (8:27)?
How can good intentions lead to spiritual compromise?

chapterList.title: Abimelech
chapterList.summary: Gideon’s son Abimelech murders seventy brothers to become king at Shechem. Only Jotham escapes and tells a parable of trees choosing a thornbush for king. God repays Abimelech’s evil: he is killed when a woman drops a millstone on his head.
questions: What is the point of Jotham’s parable (9:7–15)?
How does God bring justice in this chapter (9:56–57)?
What does Abimelech show about grasping for power?

chapterList.title: Tola, Jair, and Israel’s Repentance
chapterList.summary: Tola and Jair judge Israel. Israel serves many foreign gods and is oppressed by the Philistines and Ammonites. They cry out, and God says, “Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen.” They put away their gods, and God “became impatient over the misery of Israel.”
questions: What is different about Israel’s repentance this time (10:15–16)?
What does 10:16 reveal about God’s heart?
What would genuine repentance look like for you?

chapterList.title: Jephthah
chapterList.summary: Jephthah, the son of a prostitute rejected by his brothers, becomes Gilead’s leader. He negotiates with Ammon, then defeats them, but makes a rash vow to sacrifice whatever comes out of his house first, and his only daughter comes out to meet him.
questions: How does God use a rejected outcast?
What was wrong with Jephthah’s vow?
What can we learn about speaking rashly to God (Ecclesiastes 5:2–6)?

chapterList.title: Jephthah and Ephraim; Minor Judges
chapterList.summary: Ephraim angrily complains that it was not called to fight. Jephthah’s men defeat them and identify fleeing Ephraimites by their pronunciation of “Shibboleth.” Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon judge Israel.
questions: Why did Ephraim’s pride lead to civil war?
How do small differences become dividing lines among God’s people?
How can we pursue unity (Ephesians 4:3)?

chapterList.title: Samson’s Birth Announced
chapterList.summary: Israel is oppressed by the Philistines for forty years. The angel of the LORD tells Manoah’s barren wife she will have a son who will be a Nazirite from birth and will “begin to save Israel.” The angel ascends in the altar flame, and Samson is born.
questions: What parallels do you see between Samson’s birth and other miraculous births in Scripture?
What does it mean that Samson would only “begin” to save Israel?
How does Manoah’s prayer (13:8) model parenting?

chapterList.title: Samson’s Wedding
chapterList.summary: Samson demands a Philistine wife. The Spirit enables him to tear apart a lion. At his wedding he poses a riddle; his wife betrays the answer, and Samson kills thirty Philistines to pay his debt.
questions: What warning signs about Samson’s character appear here?
How does God use even Samson’s flawed choices (14:4)?
Why is it dangerous to be led by what is “right in your eyes” (14:3)?

chapterList.title: Samson’s Revenge
chapterList.summary: When his wife is given to another man, Samson burns the Philistines’ fields with foxes and torches. The men of Judah hand him over, but the Spirit rushes on him, and he kills a thousand Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone. Then he cries out in thirst, and God provides water.
questions: Why do you think Judah was willing to hand Samson over (15:11)?
What does Samson learn about his dependence on God (15:18–19)?
How can personal revenge escalate?

chapterList.title: Samson and Delilah
chapterList.summary: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and carries off the city gates. He loves Delilah, who is paid to discover his strength’s secret. After three deceptions he tells her, his hair is cut, and “the LORD had left him.” Blinded and enslaved, he prays one last time and brings down the temple of Dagon, killing more in his death than in his life.
questions: Why do you think Samson kept returning to Delilah despite clear danger?
What does “he did not know that the LORD had left him” (16:20) warn us about?
How does God show grace in Samson’s final prayer?

chapterList.title: Micah’s Idols
chapterList.summary: Micah steals silver from his mother, returns it, and she uses it to make an idol. He sets up a shrine and hires a wandering Levite as his priest, saying, “Now I know the LORD will prosper me.”
questions: How does this story mix worship of the LORD with idolatry?
What is wrong with Micah’s assumption in 17:13?
How can we create “custom” religion today?

chapterList.title: The Danites Take Micah’s Idols
chapterList.summary: The tribe of Dan, seeking land, steals Micah’s idols and priest and conquers the peaceful city of Laish. They set up the idol, and the priest turns out to be Moses’ grandson.
questions: How does this chapter show Israel’s spiritual decline, even among Levites?
What does Micah’s cry, “You take my gods that I made” (18:24), reveal?
Why is it significant that the priest was a descendant of Moses?

chapterList.title: The Levite’s Concubine
chapterList.summary: A Levite retrieves his concubine and stays overnight in Gibeah of Benjamin. Men of the city surround the house, echoing Sodom, and the concubine is abused all night and dies. The Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
questions: How does this chapter echo Genesis 19, and what does that say about Israel?
What do you make of the Levite’s actions?
How should God’s people respond to such evil?

chapterList.title: War Against Benjamin
chapterList.summary: Israel gathers against Gibeah, but Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men. After two defeats and much weeping and fasting before the LORD, Israel defeats Benjamin, nearly wiping out the tribe.
questions: Why might Israel have lost the first two battles?
How did Benjamin’s loyalty to evil men bring disaster?
What does this chapter show about the cost of sin?

chapterList.title: Wives for Benjamin
chapterList.summary: Regretting Benjamin’s near extinction, Israel finds wives for the survivors by destroying Jabesh-gilead and allowing the men to seize dancing girls at Shiloh. The book ends: “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
questions: How do Israel’s solutions create more injustice?
Why is 21:25 a fitting summary of the whole book?
How does this ending prepare for the books of Ruth and Samuel?

tagline: A downward spiral, and the God who keeps rescuing
readingPlan: 21 chapters: one chapter a day takes 21 days; two a day takes about 11 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
